subject: Archaeology
courseTitle: Lost Cities of the Ancient World

hook.text: A hidden city carved entirely from pink sandstone cliffs sat forgotten in the Jordanian desert for centuries.

buildup.text: The Nabataeans built Petra as a trade hub controlling the incense routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean.

discovery.text: Swiss explorer Johann Burckhardt rediscovered it in 1812 by disguising himself as an Arab pilgrim.

twist.text: Only 15 percent of Petra has been excavated. Most of the city remains buried under sand and rubble.

climax.text: The Nabataeans engineered a water system that supported 30,000 people in the middle of a desert.

punchline.text: A desert city that mastered water vanished.

quiz.question: What fraction of Petra has been excavated?
options: About half of the city has been uncovered so far
Only about 15 percent has been excavated
Nearly all major structures have been fully excavated

hook.text: Palmyra was a Roman trading city in the Syrian desert ruled briefly by a queen who defied an emperor.

buildup.text: Queen Zenobia declared independence from Rome in 270 CE and conquered Egypt before Rome crushed her revolt.

discovery.text: Its colonnaded streets, temples, and tombs survived 1,700 years of abandonment in remarkable condition.

twist.text: In 2015, ISIS destroyed the Temple of Bel and other monuments, erasing what centuries of neglect could not.

climax.text: 3D scans made before the destruction are now being used to digitally reconstruct what was lost.

punchline.text: A queen defied Rome and lost. A city defied time and almost won.

quiz.question: What happened to Palmyra's ancient monuments in 2015?
options: An earthquake damaged several major structures
ISIS destroyed the Temple of Bel and other monuments
Flooding from a nearby dam submerged part of the ruins

hook.text: Ephesus was once the second-largest city in the Roman Empire. Today it sits five miles from the sea.

buildup.text: Its library held 12,000 scrolls and its theater seated 25,000 — bigger than many modern concert venues.

discovery.text: Excavations revealed public toilets with running water, heated floors, and a medical school with surgical tools.

twist.text: The city died because the harbor silted up. Without sea access, trade vanished and people left.

climax.text: The Temple of Artemis there was one of the Seven Wonders. Only a single column remains standing today.

punchline.text: A city with heated floors and flush toilets was killed by mud.

quiz.question: What caused the decline of Ephesus?
options: A massive earthquake destroyed the city's infrastructure
The harbor silted up, cutting off sea trade
A plague wiped out most of the population

hook.text: The capital of the Persian Empire was the richest city on Earth. Alexander the Great burned it down in one night.

buildup.text: Darius I built Persepolis around 515 BCE. Twenty-three nations sent tribute and are carved into its staircases.

discovery.text: The Apadana staircase shows delegates in perfect detail — hairstyles, clothing, and gifts from across the empire.

twist.text: Alexander may have burned it in a drunken rage or as revenge for Persia's destruction of Athens. Historians disagree.

climax.text: The fire preserved thousands of clay tablets by baking them hard. Destruction accidentally saved the archives.

punchline.text: The fire that destroyed an empire accidentally preserved its records forever.

quiz.question: How did the fire at Persepolis accidentally help archaeology?
options: It melted gold into a solid mass that preserved inscriptions
It baked thousands of clay tablets hard, preserving the archives
It created an ash layer that sealed artifacts from decay

hook.text: The Hittites rivaled Egypt in power. Their capital vanished so completely that nobody believed they existed.

buildup.text: Hattusa in central Turkey had six miles of walls, 31 temples, and gates flanked by stone lions and sphinxes.

discovery.text: In 1906, archaeologists found 10,000 cuneiform tablets that proved the Hittites were a major superpower.

twist.text: Among the tablets was a copy of a peace treaty with Egypt — the same treaty Ramesses II carved on his temple walls.

climax.text: A replica of that treaty hangs in the United Nations as a symbol of diplomacy. It was written over 3,200 years ago.

punchline.text: A forgotten empire wrote the peace treaty that hangs in the UN.

quiz.question: What was found among the 10,000 tablets at Hattusa?
options: The oldest known alphabet in human history
A copy of a peace treaty with Egypt, now honored at the UN
A complete record of the Trojan War from the Hittite perspective

hook.text: Nine thousand years ago, 8,000 people lived in a Turkish town with no streets. You entered your house through the roof.

buildup.text: Çatalhöyük's mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall. Residents walked across rooftops to get around.

discovery.text: There were no public buildings, no palaces, and no signs of a leader. Everyone appears to have been equal.

twist.text: The dead were buried under the living room floor. Families literally lived on top of their ancestors.

climax.text: Murals on the walls show hunting scenes, leopards, and what may be the world's oldest landscape painting.

punchline.text: The oldest town had no streets, no rulers, and no graveyards. Just rooftops.

quiz.question: What was unusual about Çatalhöyük's social structure?
options: A council of priests ruled the entire settlement
There were no public buildings, palaces, or signs of a leader
Only women were allowed to own property or make decisions

hook.text: A city in India was once richer than Rome. When it fell, the victors spent six months looting it.

buildup.text: Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire in southern India, home to 500,000 people by the 1500s.

discovery.text: Portuguese traders described streets lined with gem merchants and markets selling Arabian horses.

twist.text: A coalition of Muslim sultanates defeated Vijayanagara in 1565 and systematically destroyed the city.

climax.text: Over 1,600 monuments survive among the boulder-strewn landscape — temples, bazaars, and royal elephant stables.

punchline.text: It took six months to destroy a city that took 200 years to build.

quiz.question: What happened to Hampi in 1565?
options: A massive flood from the river washed away most of the city
A coalition of sultanates defeated and systematically destroyed it
The ruling dynasty abandoned it to build a new capital

hook.text: A king built his palace on top of a 600-foot rock in Sri Lanka after murdering his own father for the throne.

buildup.text: King Kashyapa I built Sigiriya around 477 CE with gardens, pools, and frescoes painted on the rock face.

discovery.text: The entrance was carved as a giant lion — visitors walked through its open jaws to reach the summit.

twist.text: When his brother returned with an army, Kashyapa rode his war elephant into a swamp and killed himself.

climax.text: The fortress became a Buddhist monastery. Monks added graffiti that is now the oldest surviving writing in Sinhalese.

punchline.text: A murdered king's fortress became a place of peace.

quiz.question: What happened to Sigiriya after King Kashyapa's death?
options: His brother demolished it completely as revenge
It became a Buddhist monastery with ancient graffiti
It was used as a military fort for the next 500 years

hook.text: A Thai city was once the largest in the world. It was bigger than London when the Burmese burned it to ash.

buildup.text: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 on an island between three rivers, with canals, temples, and global trade networks.

discovery.text: Foreign merchants from Japan, China, Persia, and Portugal had their own quarters inside the city walls.

twist.text: In 1767, the Burmese invaded and destroyed everything. They melted golden Buddhas and beheaded stone statues.

climax.text: Today, rows of headless Buddhas sit in the ruins. One famous head is tangled in the roots of a banyan tree.

punchline.text: A tree swallowed a Buddha's head. Nature finished what an army started.

quiz.question: What happened to Ayutthaya in 1767?
options: A catastrophic flood submerged the island city
The Burmese invaded and destroyed the city completely
A civil war between rival princes led to abandonment

hook.text: A Taoist monk stumbled into a sealed cave in China and found 50,000 ancient documents hidden inside.

buildup.text: Dunhuang was a key Silk Road stop. Buddhist monks carved 492 caves into the cliffs and filled them with art.

discovery.text: The Library Cave, sealed around 1000 CE, contained the world's oldest printed book — the Diamond Sutra from 868 CE.

twist.text: British explorer Aurel Stein bought thousands of manuscripts for a tiny fee. China calls it cultural theft.

climax.text: The documents are now split between London, Paris, Beijing, and St. Petersburg. No single place holds them all.

punchline.text: A monk opened a cave. The world's oldest printed book fell out.

quiz.question: What was found in the sealed Library Cave at Dunhuang?
options: Thousands of jade artifacts from the Han Dynasty
50,000 documents including the world's oldest printed book
Silk garments preserved in perfect condition

topics.title: Bagan: Land of Ten Thousand Temples

hook.text: A plain in Myanmar holds over 2,000 Buddhist temples built in just 250 years. Kings competed to build the most.

buildup.text: Between 1000 and 1300 CE, Bagan's rulers built more than 10,000 temples across 26 square miles.

discovery.text: The Ananda Temple contains four standing Buddhas, each 31 feet tall, facing the four cardinal directions.

twist.text: A Mongol invasion in 1287 ended the building frenzy. Earthquakes later toppled many of the remaining temples.

climax.text: Myanmar's controversial restorations have added concrete to ancient brick, sparking debate among archaeologists.

punchline.text: Ten thousand temples rose in 250 years. Two thousand still stand.

quiz.question: What ended the temple-building era at Bagan?
options: The royal treasury ran out of funds
A Mongol invasion in 1287 ended the building period
Buddhist monks declared that no more temples were needed

topics.title: Nan Madol: The Venice of the Pacific

hook.text: On a tiny island in Micronesia, an ancient city was built on 92 artificial islands linked by canals.

buildup.text: Nan Madol was built from basalt columns, some weighing 50 tons, stacked like Lincoln Logs on coral reefs.

discovery.text: The Saudeleur dynasty ruled from here for 500 years. It was the political center of all Pohnpei.

twist.text: Nobody knows how they moved 750,000 tons of basalt to the site. There were no wheels, pulleys, or draft animals.

climax.text: When the dynasty fell around 1628, the city was abandoned to the jungle and the sea. It is now sinking.

punchline.text: A city built on the ocean is slowly returning to it.

quiz.question: What mystery surrounds the construction of Nan Madol?
options: The builders used a type of concrete unknown to modern science
Nobody knows how 750,000 tons of basalt were moved without wheels or animals
The basalt columns appear to have been imported from a continent far away

hook.text: The largest city in the ancient Americas had 100,000 residents. Nobody knows what its builders called themselves.

buildup.text: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun is the third-largest pyramid on Earth, built around 100 CE near modern Mexico City.

discovery.text: The city was planned on a grid with a two-mile central avenue. It had apartment complexes and a sewer system.

twist.text: Around 550 CE, the city was deliberately burned from the inside. Evidence suggests an internal revolt, not invasion.

climax.text: A robot exploring a tunnel under the Pyramid found liquid mercury and thousands of golden orbs in 2014.

punchline.text: A nameless people built an empire and burned it down themselves.

quiz.question: What evidence suggests Teotihuacan was destroyed from within?
options: Foreign weapons were found in the ruins
The city was burned from the inside, pointing to an internal revolt
Written records describe a civil war between priests and warriors

topics.title: Tikal: Skyscraper City of the Maya

hook.text: A Maya city with skyscraper pyramids rising above the jungle canopy lay hidden in Guatemala for centuries.

buildup.text: Tikal housed up to 90,000 people and dominated the Maya lowlands from roughly 200 to 900 CE.

discovery.text: Temple IV rises 212 feet — the tallest pre-Columbian structure in the Americas. It was built around 741 CE.

twist.text: Tikal fought a bitter war with the rival city Calakmul. The conflict shaped Maya politics for centuries.

climax.text: LiDAR scans revealed 60,000 hidden structures around Tikal, showing the city was far larger than anyone imagined.

punchline.text: The jungle hid a city for a thousand years. Lasers found it in a day.

quiz.question: What did LiDAR technology reveal about Tikal?
options: The pyramids were built over natural rock formations
60,000 hidden structures showed the city was far larger than expected
Underground tunnels connected all major temples

topics.title: Chan Chan: The Largest Adobe City

hook.text: The largest mud-brick city ever built is slowly dissolving in the rain on Peru's northern coast.

buildup.text: Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimú Empire, covering eight square miles and housing 60,000 people by 1400 CE.

discovery.text: Its walls are covered in intricate friezes of fish, birds, and waves — all carved into dried mud.

twist.text: The Inca conquered the Chimú in 1470 by diverting their water supply. No battle was needed — just thirst.

climax.text: El Niño rains are eroding the city faster each decade. Climate change may destroy what the Inca could not.

punchline.text: An empire fell to thirst. Its capital is falling to rain.

quiz.question: How did the Inca conquer the Chimú at Chan Chan?
options: They laid siege for three years until food ran out
They diverted the city's water supply, defeating them with thirst
They used superior bronze weapons to overwhelm mud-brick walls

topics.title: Palenque: Maya Art at Its Finest

hook.text: Deep in the Mexican jungle, a Maya king's tomb was sealed under a pyramid for over 1,300 years.

buildup.text: Palenque's Temple of Inscriptions held the longest Maya text known — 617 hieroglyphic blocks covering the walls.

discovery.text: In 1952, Alberto Ruz found a hidden staircase inside the temple leading down to King Pakal's jade-covered coffin.

twist.text: Pakal's carved sarcophagus lid became famous when conspiracy theorists claimed it showed him piloting a spaceship.

climax.text: Scholars showed the carving depicts Pakal descending into the underworld — standard Maya afterlife imagery.

punchline.text: A king entered the underworld on a stone lid. The internet sent him to space.

quiz.question: What does Pakal's sarcophagus lid actually depict according to scholars?
options: A detailed star map showing Maya astronomical knowledge
Pakal descending into the underworld in standard Maya afterlife imagery
A scene of conquest showing Palenque's victory over rival cities

hook.text: A city in Peru was thriving at the same time as the Egyptian pyramids. It had no pottery, no weapons, and no war.

buildup.text: Caral was built around 2600 BCE, making it the oldest known city in the Americas by a wide margin.

discovery.text: It has six large platform mounds, sunken plazas, and a residential area — but zero evidence of warfare.

twist.text: Archaeologists found quipus — knotted string records — which were thought to have been invented 3,000 years later by.

climax.text: Caral challenges the idea that civilization requires war. This society built monuments on trade, not conquest.

punchline.text: The oldest American city had pyramids but no army. Peace was its foundation.

quiz.question: What makes Caral unusual compared to other early civilizations?
options: It was built entirely underground to avoid detection
There is zero evidence of warfare — it appears to have been a peaceful society
It was exclusively a religious site with no permanent residents

hook.text: At 12,600 feet above sea level in Bolivia, an ancient city defied logic by thriving where crops barely grow.

buildup.text: Tiwanaku flourished from 500 to 1000 CE near Lake Titicaca, with monumental stone architecture and raised fields.

discovery.text: The Gate of the Sun is carved from a single block of andesite, featuring a central figure scholars still debate.

twist.text: The Inca claimed Tiwanaku was where the world began. They borrowed heavily from its art and mythology.

climax.text: A prolonged drought around 1000 CE dried up the farmland. The city was abandoned within a generation.

punchline.text: A civilization that thrived in thin air was brought down by thin rain.

quiz.question: What likely caused Tiwanaku's collapse around 1000 CE?
options: The Inca conquered and forcibly relocated the population
A prolonged drought dried up the farmland
A volcanic eruption made the region uninhabitable

hook.text: A volcanic eruption in 1600 BCE buried a Greek island town under 200 feet of ash — and preserved it perfectly.

buildup.text: Akrotiri on Santorini had three-story buildings, indoor plumbing, and vibrant wall frescoes 1,000 years before Athens.

discovery.text: Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos began excavating in 1967 and found streets, furniture, and artwork intact.

twist.text: No bodies were found anywhere. The residents apparently evacuated before the eruption — they saw it coming.

climax.text: Some scholars believe the eruption of Santorini inspired Plato's legend of Atlantis swallowed by the sea.

punchline.text: A city vanished in fire. It may have become the most famous legend ever told.

quiz.question: Why were no bodies found at Akrotiri?
options: The volcanic heat completely destroyed all organic remains
The residents apparently evacuated before the eruption
Grave robbers removed all human remains centuries ago

hook.text: An entire Egyptian port city lay hidden under the Mediterranean Sea for 1,200 years before divers found it.

buildup.text: Heracleion was Egypt's main trading port before Alexandria was built. Greek historians described it as magnificent.

discovery.text: In 2000, Franck Goddio found temples, giant statues, and 64 ships lying on the seabed in Abu Qir Bay.

twist.text: The city sank because it was built on unstable clay. Earthquakes and rising seas did the rest over centuries.

climax.text: Divers pulled up a five-meter granite statue of a pharaoh from the mud — perfectly preserved by the cold dark water.

punchline.text: The sea swallowed a city whole and kept it in near-perfect condition.

quiz.question: Why did the ancient city of Heracleion sink?
options: A massive tsunami overwhelmed the city in a single event
It was built on unstable clay that gave way during earthquakes
Rising sea levels from melting glaciers flooded the coastline

hook.text: Just off the coast of southern Greece, a 5,000-year-old city sits in 12 feet of water. You can snorkel over it.

buildup.text: Pavlopetri dates to around 2800 BCE — older than the Pyramids. It has streets, houses, and a cemetery.

discovery.text: Oceanographer Nicholas Flemming discovered it in 1967. It is the oldest known submerged city in the world.

twist.text: It likely sank due to earthquakes around 1000 BCE. The seabed preserved walls that wind and rain would have erased.

climax.text: 3D mapping in 2009 revealed the full city plan: 15 buildings, tombs, and streets — a complete Bronze Age town.

punchline.text: The oldest sunken city is in snorkeling depth. History is 12 feet below.

quiz.question: Why is Pavlopetri historically significant?
options: It contains the only underwater temple ever discovered
It is the oldest known submerged city in the world
It was the capital of the Minoan civilization

topics.title: Port Royal: The Wickedest City on Earth

hook.text: Jamaica's pirate capital sank into the sea during an earthquake in 1692. The church bell still tolled underwater.

buildup.text: Port Royal was the richest and most notorious city in the Caribbean — a haven for pirates, rum, and vice.

discovery.text: Divers found a pocket watch stopped at 11:43 AM — the exact moment the earthquake struck on June 7, 1692.

twist.text: The city sat on loose sand. Liquefaction turned the ground to liquid, swallowing two-thirds of the town in minutes.

climax.text: Preachers called it divine punishment for sin. Survivors rebuilt — and the new city sank again in a 1907 earthquake.

punchline.text: God sank the pirate city. They rebuilt. It sank again.

quiz.question: What artifact helped pinpoint the exact time of Port Royal's earthquake?
options: A ship's log found in the harbor with the date and time
A pocket watch stopped at 11:43 AM on June 7, 1692
A church clock found still ticking underwater

hook.text: Hindu scripture says the god Krishna built a golden city that sank beneath the ocean. Then divers found ruins there.

buildup.text: The Mahabharata describes Dwarka as Krishna's kingdom, swallowed by the sea after his death.

discovery.text: Marine archaeologists found stone walls, anchors, and artifacts off Gujarat's coast dating to around 1500 BCE.

twist.text: The finds match the legendary location but cannot prove the mythological story. Faith and science meet but do not agree.

climax.text: Millions of Hindu pilgrims visit the modern temple at Dwarka, believing the ancient city lies just offshore.

punchline.text: A myth described a sunken city. Divers found one in the same spot.

quiz.question: What complicates the archaeological interpretation of underwater Dwarka?
options: The ruins are too deep for divers to study properly
The finds match the location but cannot prove the mythological story
Modern construction has destroyed most of the underwater evidence

hook.text: Everyone knows Pompeii. Fewer know its neighbor Herculaneum, which was even better preserved — under 60 feet of rock.

buildup.text: While Pompeii was buried in ash, Herculaneum was entombed by a pyroclastic surge that carbonized everything instantly.

discovery.text: The extreme heat preserved wood, food, fabric, and even a library of carbonized scrolls still being read today.

twist.text: 300 skeletons were found on the beach — people waiting for boats that never came as the eruption overtook them.

climax.text: AI is now reading the burnt scrolls using X-ray scanning. Lost works of ancient philosophy are being recovered.

punchline.text: A volcano burned a library. Two thousand years later, AI is reading the ashes.

quiz.question: How is modern technology recovering Herculaneum's burnt scrolls?
options: Chemical treatments are unrolling and bleaching the scrolls
AI reads the carbonized text using X-ray scanning
3D printing recreates the scrolls from fragment photographs

hook.text: Plato described Atlantis as a powerful island that sank in a single day. People have been looking ever since.

buildup.text: Over 11,000 books and articles have been written about Atlantis. Proposed locations span every continent.

discovery.text: Most scholars believe Plato invented Atlantis as a parable about the dangers of pride and imperial ambition.

twist.text: Some archaeologists point to the Minoan eruption of Santorini as the real event behind the fictional story.

climax.text: Despite zero archaeological evidence, Atlantis remains the most searched-for lost city in history.

punchline.text: The most famous lost city probably never existed. We keep looking anyway.

quiz.question: What do most scholars believe about Plato's Atlantis?
options: It was a real city destroyed by a volcanic eruption
He invented it as a parable about pride and imperial ambition
It was a coded description of ancient Egypt

topics.title: Percy Fawcett and the Lost City of Z

hook.text: A British explorer vanished in the Amazon in 1925 while searching for a lost city he called 'Z.' He was never found.

buildup.text: Colonel Percy Fawcett believed a sophisticated civilization once thrived in the Brazilian jungle. Everyone laughed.

discovery.text: Fawcett, his son, and a friend entered the Xingu region and sent their last letter on May 29, 1925.

twist.text: Modern LiDAR and satellite imagery have since found massive earthworks and planned settlements in the exact region.

climax.text: Fawcett was right about complex Amazonian civilizations. He just could not prove it with 1925 technology.

punchline.text: He died looking for a lost city. Technology proved he was right 90 years later.

quiz.question: What has modern technology revealed about Fawcett's theory?
options: The Amazon was always too hostile for any civilization
LiDAR found massive earthworks in the exact region he explored
His lost city of Z was actually a misidentified Inca outpost

hook.text: Sarah Parcak finds lost cities from space using satellite imagery. She has located 17 potential pyramids from her desk.

buildup.text: Infrared satellite images detect buried walls because compacted mud retains moisture differently than surrounding soil.

discovery.text: Parcak identified the lost city of Tanis in the Nile Delta and a possible Viking site in Newfoundland from satellite.

twist.text: She launched a citizen-science platform where anyone can analyze satellite images to find unknown archaeological sites.

climax.text: Satellite archaeology is now used to monitor looting in real time — tracking illegal digs in conflict zones like Syria.

punchline.text: Lost cities hide underground. Satellites see what shovels cannot.

quiz.question: How do satellites detect buried structures?
options: They use radar to bounce signals off underground walls
Infrared images detect moisture differences between compacted mud and soil
Visible-light cameras spot color changes in vegetation above ruins

hook.text: A laser technology that can see through dense forest canopy is rewriting the history of entire civilizations.

buildup.text: LiDAR fires millions of laser pulses from aircraft. Some pass through leaves and bounce off the ground below.

discovery.text: In Cambodia, LiDAR revealed that Angkor was the largest pre-industrial city on Earth — far bigger than maps showed.

twist.text: In Guatemala, it found 60,000 Maya structures, roads, and farms that no one had seen despite decades of ground surveys.

climax.text: LiDAR is finding so many sites so fast that there are not enough archaeologists to investigate them all.

punchline.text: We spent centuries searching jungles on foot. Lasers did more in a week.

quiz.question: What did LiDAR reveal about the Maya civilization in Guatemala?
options: The Maya had no roads or infrastructure between cities
60,000 structures, roads, and farms invisible from ground surveys
Maya cities were much smaller than previously estimated

hook.text: Every lost city was once someone's home. They disappear for surprisingly few reasons — and we keep repeating them.

buildup.text: Drought killed Tiwanaku. Earthquakes sank Pavlopetri. Volcanic ash buried Akrotiri. Nature is the top destroyer.

discovery.text: War destroyed Palmyra and Hampi. Political collapse emptied Teotihuacan. Human violence ranks second.

twist.text: Some cities simply moved. Constantinople did not disappear — it became Istanbul. Cities evolve, they do not always die.

climax.text: Climate change now threatens modern coastal cities with the same fate as ancient ones — rising seas and shifting.

punchline.text: Lost cities are warnings written in stone. We rarely read them.

quiz.question: What is the most common cause of cities being lost to history?
options: Economic decline and loss of trade routes
Natural disasters like drought, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions
Conquest by rival empires who demolished the structures

hook.text: Conquistadors searched decades for a city of gold. It never existed, but the hunt shaped a continent.

buildup.text: The legend began with a Muisca chief who coated himself in gold dust and dove into a lake.

discovery.text: Lake Guatavita in Colombia was partially drained. Gold objects were found in the mud.

twist.text: El Dorado was a ritual, not a place. The Spanish turned a ceremony into a fantasy.

climax.text: The search drove the conquest of the Amazon and the destruction of real empires.

punchline.text: The city of gold never existed. The search for it destroyed real ones.

quiz.question: What was El Dorado originally?
options: A vast underground city filled with Aztec gold
A Muisca ritual where a gold-covered chief dove into a lake
A Spanish fort built to store stolen treasure
